evidence.label: The weak pinned planar distance theorem
A power saving for planar unit distances

headline: Proves almost every point in a large planar set sees nearly n distances, and lowers the unit-distance exponent 4/3.
scope: Two results on finite point sets in the plane: distinct distances seen from single points, and the number of pairs at distance one.
plain: Put n points in the plane and stand at one of them. Erdős asked in 1957 whether some point always sees almost n different distances to the others. The first paper proves more: almost every point does. The second paper limits how many pairs can be exactly one unit apart, lowering a 1984 exponent of 4/3 by a fixed amount. A computer proof checker has formal versions of both main results.
doesNot: This does not give explicit rates or constants. The first theorem has no rate of decay, and the second states no value for its new exponent. It also does not close the gap with the known lower bounds for unit distances.
origin: This result comes from an unreleased OpenAI model, published in the openai/math release on 6 October 2026.

scorecard.firstStepBy: Paul Erdős, distinct-distance and repeated-distance problems
scorecard.significanceWhy: It resolves Erdős's weak pinned distance conjecture and gives the first fixed power saving over the 1984 unit-distance bound, both with Lean statements.

explanation:
Take a 4 by 4 square grid of 16 points, one unit apart. Stand at a corner and measure the distance to each other point. The squared distances take 9 different values: 1, 2, 4, 5, 8, 9, 10, 13 and 18. Now stand at the point one step in from that corner, diagonally. From there you see only 5 different distances. Next count pairs of points exactly one unit apart. Each row has 3 such pairs, and so does each column, giving 24 pairs.

Erdős started both questions in 1946[1]. The first asks how many distances a single point, called a pin, must see. The weak pinned conjecture says some point sees at least n^(1−ε) distances, for any small ε and large n[2]. Erdős stated this in 1957[2]. The best earlier pinned bound reached every exponent below about 0.864[3]. Some points can see very few distances. For points on a circle plus its centre, the centre sees only one[4].

The first paper proves the conjecture in a stronger form. For any fixed ε, all but a vanishing fraction of the n points see at least n^(1−ε) distances[5]. No assumption on spacing or position is needed, but the paper gives no rate[6]. The obstacle is that distances are real numbers with no structure to count. The proof moves each set into a number field, a system of algebraic numbers, without changing any equality between distances[7].

The second question asks for u(n), the largest number of unit-distance pairs among n points. For the grid above, 24 is well below 16^(4/3), about 40.3. Spencer, Szemerédi and Trotter proved u(n) is at most a constant times n^(4/3) in 1984[8]. An OpenAI construction already showed u(n) can exceed n^(1+ε) for some sizes[9]. The second paper shows u(n) is at most C·n^β for some fixed β below 4/3[10]. Its proof combines incidence counting with entropy and heights of algebraic numbers[11].

How sure is this? Lean, a computer proof checker, has formal statements of both main theorems. So the papers prove them, as far as the Lean statements match the papers. The first paper gives no rate, and the second states no value for β. No specialist review of either paper is published.
hypeCheck: Landmark if it holds up: it settles a named Erdős conjecture and improves a 1984 exponent, with Lean statements for both. Neither result has explicit constants, and no specialist review is published.

A pair of points exactly one unit apart.
